item.title: The Inconsistency That Wasn’t
item.dc:creator: Steven Ponce
item.description:
The Spark

Makeover Monday’s Week 47 challenge featured a 19 × 19 heatmap from the CAPphrase project. Each cell shows how often respondents judged one probability phrase higher than another. Cells near 50/50 are colored red, and the legend calls them “most inconsistent.”

I had explored this dataset earlier, in TidyTuesday Week 10 (Lost in the Middle), looking at the numeric estimates people give each phrase. This time the label raised a different question: inconsistent at what level, the crowd or the individual? A 50/50 cell says the crowd split. It doesn’t say that any one person wavered.

The Detour

The data held a way to test that. Each of 5,174 respondents made ten comparisons, and comparison 10 repeated comparison 1 with the two phrases on swapped sides. The original chart’s 342 cells reproduce exactly only when those repeated answers are included.

That repeat separates two questions:

  • Between people: how often do two different respondents answer the same pair differently?
  • Within a person: how often does one respondent change their own answer?

The heatmap shows how the crowd answered. Its label suggests something about how individuals behave. Those are two different questions, and only the repeat can speak to the second.

I limited the test to the 18 pairs that divided the crowd, where the more popular answer accounted for 50 to 70% of first responses. That left 612 respondents who saw one of those pairs twice.

The Check

The within-person rate is observed: the share of those 612 whose second answer differed from their first. The between-person rate has to be estimated. If a share p of respondents pick one phrase, two independently drawn responses disagree with probability 2p(1 − p).

Two decisions mattered.

First, the benchmark could not reuse the answers it was meant to evaluate. My first calculation drew p from answers that included comparison 1, the first half of the repeated question. I corrected that by estimating p from comparisons 2 to 9 only. The correction kept the answers used to estimate crowd disagreement separate from those used to measure individual reversals.

Second, the selection rule constrained the benchmark before any result arrived:

between <- function(p) 2 * p * (1 - p)
between(c(0.50, 0.60, 0.70))

# 0.50 0.48 0.42   <- pairs split 50-70% can only land between 42% and 50%

The benchmark was always going to be close to 50%. Its exact value, 46.5%, comes from the data. It is a yardstick, not an independently observed disagreement rate.

The Chart

Asked the same pair again, 12.3% of the 612 changed their answer, against a 46.5% benchmark for two different people.

The first version of this chart failed my own comprehension review. I read the two bars as two groups of people, the percentages had no stated meaning, and the intervals had no labels. The final version names two answering situations instead, “two different people, each answering once” and “the same person, asked again a few questions later,” and says what each interval is.

The limits stay in view. The repeat came nine comparisons later in the same sitting, so memory may have held the change rate down. The sides were always swapped, with an unknown effect. Most respondents kept their original answer within this short quiz. That says nothing about whether answers would hold over weeks, or about why people disagree.

The Takeaway

A statistic can be computed correctly and still be given the wrong meaning. Before attaching a word like “inconsistent” to a number, check that the unit of analysis can support it.

A split crowd describes the group. Individual inconsistency requires evidence from the same person. This dataset happened to contain the repeat that could supply it. Most datasets don’t, and then the honest move is to describe the split and stop there.

item.title: The Correlation I Almost Trusted
item.dc:creator: Steven Ponce
item.description:
The Spark

This week’s TidyTuesday dataset asked a deceptively simple question: how long does a barista have to work to afford the cappuccino they just made? Across 87 countries, that question quickly turned into something more interesting: why does the index vary so much from one country to another?

The Detour

Early on, the data seemed to tell a clean story. The Cappuccino Index (minutes of work per cappuccino) correlated much more strongly with wages than with coffee prices:

  • Index vs. wage: ρ = −0.927
  • Index vs. coffee price: ρ = −0.353

I had a headline half-written in my head: it’s the wage, not the coffee.

Then I stopped, because it felt too convenient. The index isn’t an independent measurement – it’s defined as:

index = 60 × price / wage

Wage is sitting in the formula’s own denominator. So a strong negative association between wage and the index isn’t surprising – part of that relationship is built into the metric itself. The same problem applies, in the other direction, to price. Comparing those two correlations doesn’t cleanly tell me which ingredient is doing more of the work.

The Check

I needed a comparison that didn’t use the index itself. So I asked a simpler question: which ingredient varies more across countries?

driver_diag |>
  summarise(
    sd_log_price = sd(log(mean_price)),
    sd_log_wage  = sd(log(mean_wage))
  )

# sd_log_price: 0.381
# sd_log_wage:  0.949   <- about 2.5× the price dispersion

What survived was a narrower observation. On the log scale, wages show about 2.5× the cross-country dispersion of coffee prices – a much more defensible statement than “it’s the wage, not the coffee.”

The Chart

That detour changed the chart. Plotting wage against price directly makes both ingredients visible instead of hiding them inside a single ratio.

The Takeaway

When a metric is built from the variables you’re comparing it with, inspect the formula before interpreting the correlations.

A strong relationship may partly reflect the metric’s construction rather than a new empirical finding. Stepping away from the index and comparing the ingredients directly led to a narrower claim I could actually defend.
